content_voiceover: This table summarizes factor replacement dosing across different clinical scenarios, joint or muscle bleeds, life or limb threatening bleeds, preoperative dosing, and prophylaxis, for the major factor concentrates. The key pharmacokinetic rules of thumb are boxed in orange. For standard factor eight, each unit per kilogram raises factor activity by about two percent, so a fifty unit per kilogram dose roughly doubles circulating factor eight. Extended half-life factor eight, like FVIII-FC, follows the same two percent rule but only needs redosing every eight to twelve hours instead of every eight to twelve for standard product, reflecting its longer half-life. For factor nine, plasma-derived product raises activity by about one percent per unit per kilogram, while recombinant factor nine only raises it zero point six to zero point eight percent per unit per kilogram, because recombinant FIX has a larger volume of distribution and lower recovery than plasma-derived FIX. This recovery difference is a classic board question. Both factor nine products are redosed every twelve to twenty-four hours given the longer half-life of factor nine compared to factor eight.
keypoints: FVIII: 1 IU/kg raises activity by about 2 percent, redosed every 8-12 hours
pdFIX: 1 IU/kg raises activity by about 1 percent
rFIX: 1 IU/kg raises activity by only 0.6-0.8 percent due to lower in vivo recovery
FIX products redosed every 12-24 hours, reflecting a longer half-life than FVIII
keypoint_voiceover: Key points to memorize. Standard factor eight raises activity about two percent per unit per kilogram and is redosed every eight to twelve hours. Plasma-derived factor nine raises activity about one percent per unit per kilogram. Recombinant factor nine only raises it zero point six to zero point eight percent, because of lower in vivo recovery, a classic exam pitfall. And factor nine products, whether plasma-derived or recombinant, are redosed every twelve to twenty-four hours, reflecting factor nine's longer half-life.
